standard.title: People shape places
standard.description: the influence of people, including First Nations Australians and people in other countries, on the characteristics of a place
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K05 (Importance of environments): Students explain the importance of environments and the connections people have to them. Students understand that places have natural and human characteristics.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the influence of people, including First Nations Australians and people in other countries, on the characteristics of a place, evaluating both positive and negative effects of human influence.

nodes.label: How people change place characteristics
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that people influence the characteristics of places through land use, resource management and development decisions, and give examples of how this happens.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two ways people change the characteristics of a place.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of ways people change place characteristics: vegetation clearance, fencing, urban development, drainage, irrigation, farming, introduction of livestock, mining, and forest plantations, with examples drawn from Australian contexts.
wider: Investigate how the characteristics of a local place have changed over time by comparing historical and current photographs, maps or records
Explore examples of human influence on place characteristics in countries in Asia, Europe or North America, and compare with Australian examples
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand only physical/natural characteristics of places (from earlier years) need to clearly grasp that human decisions actively and intentionally reshape places. This conceptual shift from 'places have characteristics' to 'people create characteristics' is foundational for the evaluative work in subsequent nodes.

response_modes.reason: Use a 'before and after' framework to make the human influence visible — explicitly connecting the decision (what people did) to the characteristic change (what the place became).

success_criteria: Students name at least two ways people influence the characteristics of places.
Students give a specific example for at least one of these influences.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and place management
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australians have influenced place characteristics through land and resource management practices such as firestick farming.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one way First Nations Australians managed land or resources and describe the effect on the place's characteristics.
nodes.typical_width: Explain First Nations Australian land management practices including firestick farming, and describe how these practices sustained environments and shaped place characteristics over thousands of years.
wider: Investigate a specific First Nations community's land management practices and compare them with post-colonial land use in the same area
Explore how contemporary land management in Australia is incorporating First Nations knowledge and practices, and the effect this is having on the characteristics of specific places

response_modes.reason: First Nations land management is a distinct and important context — treating it as equivalent enrichment to other land use examples risks reducing it to tokenism. Give it dedicated time and treat the knowledge system as significant in its own right.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The elaborations foreground firestick farming and contemporary applications of First Nations land management — this is pedagogically significant content with genuine breadth potential including contemporary relevance.
success_criteria: Students explain at least one First Nations land management practice and describe its effect on a place.
Students distinguish First Nations land management from post-colonial approaches in at least one example.

nodes.label: Positive and negative influences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate positive and negative human influences on place characteristics, giving examples of each and explaining why some actions are considered beneficial or harmful.
nodes.minimum_width: Give one example each of a positive and a negative human influence on a place and explain why each is categorised that way.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate a range of positive influences (e.g. reforestation, land-care, rehabilitation of mining sites) and negative influences (e.g. vegetation clearance, urban sprawl, pollution) on place characteristics, and explain the criteria used to categorise them.
wider: Investigate a specific land rehabilitation project (e.g. rehabilitated mine site, wetland restoration) and evaluate its success in restoring place characteristics
Examine an example of positive or negative human influence on places in another country (including Asia, Europe or North America) and compare the context and consequences with an Australian example

response_modes.reason: Evaluation of positive/negative influence depends heavily on whose perspective is centred — present multiple stakeholder views (environmental, economic, community) to avoid oversimplified good/bad categorisation.

success_criteria: Students give at least one example each of a positive and negative human influence on a place.
Students explain the reasoning behind categorising each influence as positive or negative.

nodes.label: Evaluating human influence on place characteristics
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the influence of diverse groups of people on the characteristics of a place, evaluating the range of positive and negative effects and considering different perspectives on those effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the influence of at least two different groups of people on a place and evaluate whether the overall effect has been positive or negative.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the influence of multiple groups (including First Nations Australians, colonists/settlers, and people in other countries) on the characteristics of a place, evaluating the economic, environmental and social effects and acknowledging that perspectives on these effects differ.
wider: Construct an argument for a particular course of action to manage human influence on a specific place, drawing on evidence about current and historical impacts
Evaluate the long-term sustainability of current human influences on a chosen place, considering what characteristics might be lost if current practices continue

response_modes.reason: This node brings together the full range of human influences, including First Nations, colonial and international contexts, into an evaluative account. Use a structured comparison or evaluation matrix to support synthesis.

success_criteria: Students explain the influence of at least two different groups on the characteristics of a place.
Students evaluate the positive and/or negative effects of these influences with reference to evidence.
Students acknowledge that different groups may view the same influence differently.
